note: ERA 30. L2 (Q155 -> A133) and D8b (Q158 -> A136), measured together with an arm each. build.bulldoze 1 -> 5: buildCost is idiv(base x buildCostPercent, 100), so at a base of 1 clearing ground cost NOTHING at relaxed (70%) and steady (90%) - the default - from slice 1.3 until X3a asked an approved request to charge the demolition and the compensation and the demolition came to zero. Kjell chose the price over a floor under the arithmetic: relaxed 3, steady 4, demanding 6, and no other price in this table moves. In the same era the TOOLS load data/ the way the page and the server do (tools/lib/content.mjs), the quests above all - engine/quests.js has no mirror, so CATALOGUE was empty and every number this project had measured came from a city in which no quest could fire, while a browser has 21; quests pay money and set rank, so it is a rule change. sim_sweep 200 games x 25 years per configuration, three arms (reports/balance-era30.md and balance-era30-arm-{bulldoze,quests}): BOTH CHANGES ARE ECONOMICALLY INVISIBLE to the deputy's city. Population 1811/1710/1543/1572 against era 29's 1811/1710/1545/1572; treasury 13,600-17,500 higher on four to five million, which is the quests' reward money less the price. With disasters OFF the price arm's treasury is byte-identical to the null, because the deputy only ever bulldozes to clear a ruin (B1a). On demanding, where there is no slack, the price costs six residents of 1,545 and the quests cost two. 200 of 200 cities alive in every arm. ERA 29. B14: the deputy lays a street only where there is not already one within `deputy.blockTiles` tiles of most of the run. It laid a run wherever its cursor stood and the cursor hops -2..2 tiles across, so two streets could be laid side by side: a played 64 came out 31-40% road against the references' 4-13% of a frame, and S15c had already ruled out the renderer's half by measuring it (narrowing the carriageway moved the share 0.7 points, because the grey at town zoom is the grid's SPACING). Measured on three seeds: road share 31.2/39.5/34.4% -> 23.3/27.7/18.3%, side-by-side pairs roughly halved. Population moves both ways per seed, which is what the sweep is for. ERA 28. L1 (A130): borrowing is built. takeLoan and repayLoan, a debt on the player record, a ceiling by RANK (4k/12k/30k/60k) and interest of 6 per thousand per month billed with the utilities. The era moves because a player record now carries a hashed field, so every save and every fixture hash moves - and the SWEEP should not move at all, because the deputy never borrows (test/deputy.test.js asserts it over forty years). That is the claim era 28 exists to check: identical medians against era 27 means the ladder is the player's alone. ERA 27. B13 (A61): weather causes things. A storm throws one lightning strike through the ordinary fire system - it spreads, is fought by fire cover and burns out like any other fire - and a DOWNPOUR is the eighth disaster: it floods the tiles with a pipe under them, and only in a city whose water demand is already over what its pumps make, which is a question the engine had already answered in supply.water. The era moves because the roll itself moved: chooseKind now draws from eight kinds, so every disaster in every city after the first roll is a different disaster, and era 26's numbers are void rather than roughly comparable. Measured: disaster_soak 200 games x 25 years, the downpour fires 52 times, every type fires, no unrecoverable cities. ERA 26. A121 (Q143): the deputy goes looking for a crossing. S13 gave it the ability to span a river its block happens to meet; this is the rule that SEEKS one, which is the first deputy rule whose purpose is to reach land it does not own. The scan is over the town's own flooded tiles rather than the map, four directions from each, up to build.bridgeSpan tiles of water, landing on three tiles of ground that are ours to pave - and it only counts as a crossing if there is room beyond it: deputy.bridgeNeedsRoom free unzoned tiles within bridgeRoomReach of where the bridge lands. Chosen from a ladder over eight 64 rolling seeds, 25 years: never -> 1,740 residents and 233 buildings with 93 water tiles paved incidentally; at 900 with room 40 -> 1,830 and 242 with 142 and three crossings sought; at 400 with room 40 -> 1,829 and 243; at 400 with room 20 -> 1,789 and 235; at 900 with room 20 -> 1,790 and 235. The threshold barely matters and the ROOM does: demanding real land on the far side is what makes the far bank worth anything, which is the question Q143 asked. And the answer to that question is NOT the 200-game sweep, which reads flat - relaxed 1,764 to 1,749, steady 1,604 to 1,600, demanding 1,520 to 1,511, nodisasters 1,580 to 1,565, with the same one demanding city of two hundred ending empty as at era 25. It is the per-seed arm: over twelve 64 rolling seeds the rule fires in TWO, every city where it does not fire is unchanged to the resident, and the two where it does go 1,506 to 1,866 on average - seed 202 alone goes 1,483 to 2,202, which is half a city again. So the far bank is worth a quarter of a city where the town is hemmed in by water, and nothing at all where it is not; the sweep reads flat because two cities in twelve are hemmed in. A rule that fires rarely and pays when it does is worth keeping, and the number that says so is the one measured where it fires. ERA 25. A120 (Q144): no building stands on a plinth taller than development.maxPlinth (8 steps, four metres). A building is seated on the lowest corner of its lot and a plinth makes up the difference (ruling 038), so a footprint across a hillside is a building buried in it with a wall of base below - which is what S12's shore shot shows at every waterline and what walkthrough counts as 'buried' (four lots on hilly 128, each sixteen steps, the walker's feet within 15 cm of a roof). One rule, both halves: placeBuilding refuses with RESULT.TOO_STEEP and lotFree refuses a grown lot, the shape ruling 046 had to fix twice. Note what the grown half can reach today: a grown footprint is at most 2x2, so its spread is one tile step, and canZone already refuses a step past maxZoneSlope (6) - under the limit. So on today's numbers it is the PLACED buildings the rule bites, which is where the measurement said the problem was: on a played hilly 128 the worst are a 3x3 coal plant at 28 steps (fourteen metres), a police headquarters at 26 and a rail station at 22. Measured on the played fixtures: hilly 128 goes from 185 buildings with a worst plinth of 28 steps to 129 with a worst of 8 and none over the limit; rolling 96 is UNMOVED at 284 buildings (its worst was already 7); flat 64 never had a spread over 1. The 200-game sweep is flat - relaxed 1,800 to 1,764, steady 1,585 to 1,604, demanding 1,541 to 1,520, nodisasters 1,568 to 1,580 - and demanding's report shows one city of two hundred ending empty against none at era 24. That city is NOT this rule: two arms over the sweep's own 200 demanding seeds, the rule off and on, give 1 dead and median 1,550 against 1 dead and median 1,548. The rule costs demanding two residents and bites hilly ground, which is where the picture was wrong. Measured with tools/sim_sweep.mjs over 200 games per configuration; see reports/balance-era25.md. ERA 24. S13 (A84, Q104, ruling 047): the deputy crosses a river. The engine has always allowed a road over water and charged build.roadOverWater for it; what it had no rule for was how FAR, so S13 adds build.bridgeSpan (6 tiles, 120 m - a river rather than a lake) and a crossing must end on dry land. That half changes nothing the deputy did, because the deputy had never crossed water at all: buildBlockAlong breaks on !isBuildable, and J3's step-along-the-run slope rule treats a water tile's elevation as its BED, so every river was also a cliff. Both are fixed here - a run spans water it can reach the far bank of, and the span does not count against the block's length, because a bridge is not street. Measured in two arms over eight 64 rolling seeds, 25 years: before, 1,694 residents and 225 buildings with ZERO road tiles on water; after, 1,749 and 238 with 124 water tiles paved over eight cities. The 200-game sweep points the other way and is the authority: relaxed's median population 1,821 to 1,800, steady 1,615 to 1,585, demanding 1,566 to 1,541, treasuries 2-4% lower - a crossing costs five times a road tile - with ZERO dead cities in every configuration, as era 23. Eight seeds say a rule fires; two hundred games say what it is worth. Note what the sweep cannot see: the 96 fixture's river is wider than six tiles nearly everywhere, so the deputy builds no bridge there at all and every renderer gate measured a city with no crossing in it - tools/lib/saturated.mjs lays one on purpose now and throws if it cannot. Measured with tools/sim_sweep.mjs over 200 games per configuration; see reports/balance-era24.md. ERA 23. J4 (A106, Q141): demanding's margin, re-cut against a real expense, and H8's lever raised to the rung it was measured for. taxYieldPercent 80 and upkeepPercent 120 were set in era 1 when a developed lot cost nothing to serve, so demanding had nothing to absorb era 21's service cost with and that lever shipped at a third of its worth. Measured over FORTY demanding cities a rung: 80/120 with the service cost doubled gives 1,207 residents and four dead cities of forty; 90/110 gives 1,516 with none, against the 1,547 demanding has today, and a p25 treasury of 1,676k against 1,616k. So the squeeze comes in by a third and economy.serviceCostPerLevel doubles to 6/12/22/35 - demanding ends where it started with a real expense inside it, and relaxed and steady pay the larger cost without the easier squeeze. 95/105 was measured and is too kind; 12/25/45/70 kills cities at every squeeze tried, which is where this lever stops. Measured with tools/sim_sweep.mjs over 200 games per configuration; see reports/balance-era23.md. ERA 22. J3 (A112, Q140): a road refuses the ground a lot refuses. Era 20 put the slope rule in canZone and placeNetwork never got it, so the city stayed off the cliff and the STREETS did not - on a played hilly 128 the deputy paved a 500% hillside to reach the next flat patch and 218 of 612 corridors came out steeper than any grading can flatten. The rule is development.maxRoadSlope, and it is NOT the lot's test: a lot refuses ground too rough to stand on (the max step to any neighbour) and a road refuses a CLIMB too steep to drive (the step between consecutive tiles of the run), because a street along a contour has a gentle grade and a steep neighbour. The first cut used the lot's test and took a played hilly city from 1,872 residents to 217. Water is exempt - a water tile's elevation is its bed, and a crossing is S13's question. Twelve steps, chosen by the GATE that A112 named: walkthrough 128 hilly is GREEN for the first time in the project (0 cliffs against 25, 20 of 177 corridors ungradeable against 218 of 612, steepest street 33.3% against 500%) and it joins the render set, which is S11's own done-when met at last. The ladder over four 64 maps a style: rolling is unmoved from 10 upward, hilly reads 147 residents at 6, 697 at 10, 1,094 at 11, 1,066 at 12, 964 at 13, 1,711 at 14 and 1,342 with no limit at all - a moderate limit beats NO limit by a quarter, because a deputy that stops at the foot of a hill builds where the city can be served. Measured with tools/sim_sweep.mjs over 200 games per configuration; see reports/balance-era22.md. ERA 21. H8 (A101, Q118): a developed lot costs the city money to serve. Every income term in this project was decoration because income ran FOUR TIMES expenses at every size and every difficulty - a steady 25-year city took 20,268 a month and spent 5,048 - and the reason was that a developed lot paid tax and cost nothing, while the only expenses were the civic buildings and a penny a road tile. economy.serviceCostPerLevel is what a lot costs per level per tile; per-TILE upkeep was tried twice and rejected twice (era 0, era 1) because it bankrupts a young town without touching a rich one, and this scales with what the city has GROWN instead. Measured as a four-rung ladder over eight cities a difficulty: at 0 the treasuries are 6,466k relaxed / 5,021k steady / 2,534k demanding; at 6/12/22/35 they are 5,837k / 4,264k / 1,258k with nobody dead; at 12/25/45/70 DEMANDING COLLAPSES from 1,644 residents to 163 with one city of eight dead. The useful range of this lever is bounded by demanding's own margin rather than by the mechanism - it pays 120% of every expense and keeps 80% of every tax, so it has nothing to absorb a new one with - J4 (A106) re-cuts it. The eight-seed ladder said 6/12/22/35 killed nobody and the 200-game SWEEP said nine demanding cities of two hundred reached a hundred residents and ended empty - never tune on five seeds, from the other direction - so the rung came down again: at 3/6/11/18, measured over FORTY demanding cities, the dead count is 0, the population is 1,618 against 1,632 and the treasury 1,955k against 2,374k. A first step, deliberately small, and the reason it is small is demanding's own margin - J4 (A106) re-cuts it and raises this. Measured with tools/sim_sweep.mjs over 200 games per configuration; see reports/balance-era21.md. ERA 20. H6 (A100, Q134): ground too steep to build on is not zoned. S11 let a junction's height move within six metres of its own land and took hilly 128 from 177 cliffs on the walked route to 30; what was left was 20 m corridors with 10 m of land between their ends, which no cutting a person would dig fixes at 15%. Kjell took the expensive option: the city is not on the cliff in the first place. development.maxZoneSlope is 6 elevation steps, which IS the street's own limit - road.maxGrade 15% of a 20 m tile is 3 m is six half-metre steps - so you may not zone ground a street could not be built on. It is canZone's rule, so it is the reducer's: one rule, the same for a player and for the deputy, answered with RESULT.TOO_STEEP rather than 'that cannot go there'. The deputy skips steep tiles when it zones, because a zoning run is a transaction and one steep tile would refuse the whole strip. Measured on three 64 maps a style, 25 years: hilly goes from population 1,015 with 505 zoned tiles to 1,872 with 334 - nearly TWICE the city, because the zoning that goes down is zoning that can be reached and served instead of scattered up a hillside - and rolling is unmoved (1,837 to 1,734 population, 301 to 293 buildings, inside three-seed noise). Measured with tools/sim_sweep.mjs over 200 games per configuration; see reports/balance-era20.md. ERA 19. H5 (A96, Q130): the deputy repairs a grid a disaster cut in two. G2 made every carrier RUN reach a live piece of grid and left the other half open - the deputy connects a building when it BUILDS it and never looks again, so a component that loses its producer stays dark for the rest of the game, and what repair there was came incidentally from new buildings' carriers. Measured by cutting every wire in one column of a 15-year city: seed 1003 darkened 84 buildings of 234 and had 54 still dark a year later; seed 404 darkened 80 and had six still dark after FIVE years. With the rule: 0 and 5 after one year, and the grid back to one component on 1003. Two defects in the first cut, both the same shape as G2's: it ran carriers out of the COAL PLANT two hundred and forty times, because a producer on an under-capacity component is itself unlit and a plant's darkness is keepSupplied's problem rather than a route to find; and it counted a turn as spent whether or not the run laid anything, so the deputy stopped doing everything else and the city it was repairing went from 84 dark to 211. connectToNetwork now reports whether it actually laid a run. Only when the city HAS the capacity: a brown-out is a shortfall to build out of, not a grid to re-stitch. Measured with tools/sim_sweep.mjs over 200 games per configuration; see reports/balance-era19.md. ERA 18. H4 (A97, Q131): the deputy dezones what it paves. It crosses its own zoned land on purpose - B9 measured that refusing to cross a zoned strip cut the sweep's population by half, because crossing one is how blocks join - and since era 15 a lot cannot grow on a road, so those tiles were zoning that had been paid for and could never be used: 591 of 1,688 on seed 1003, 639 of 1,646 on an eight-seed mean, two in five. Every path that lays road dezones under it, not only buildBlock: the rail station's access road and the ferry terminal's are connectToNetwork runs, and leaving them out left exactly ONE zoned-and-paved tile a city, which is the kind of remainder that reads as a rounding error and is a missed caller. The dead runCarrier() goes in the same commit - no caller anywhere, superseded by connectToNetwork's search, and it called apply() directly rather than issue(), so it would not have counted its own refusals. Measured with tools/sim_sweep.mjs over 200 games per configuration; see reports/balance-era18.md. ERA 17. H3 (A99, Q133/Q111): the mayor plants parks and builds police stations. The deputy has built neither for the life of the project - 0 parks and 0 police stations in a 25-year city - so every balance number this project has ever published was measured on a city that had no park to carry G3's landValueBonus and no patrol to answer B3b's crime. One rule each, both in the shape the fire station has had since B1a: a police station per deputy.buildingsPerPolice (40, mirroring the fire station exactly - same footprint, same price, same upkeep) and a park per deputy.buildingsPerPark (20, the cheapest thing in the catalogue at 60 and 2 a month). Both use (n + 1) * per <= others rather than n * per < others, which is the form T7 got wrong twice and which fires at a town of ONE building; the fire station keeps its older form deliberately, because a town wants a fire service from the first house. Measured in three arms over eight seeds, 25 years: base 1,582 population, land value 125.3, crime 1.6, 219 buildings; parks alone 1,973 / 132.4 / 1.9 / 261; police alone 1,826 / 126.1 / 2.0 / 253; both 2,082 / 135.5 / 0.8 / 305. Each rule grows the city on its own and together they take crime to half what it was - a park reaches crime through land value (A93's path) and a patrol reaches it directly. Measured with tools/sim_sweep.mjs over 200 games per configuration; see reports/balance-era17.md. ERA 16. G3 (A88, A91, Q119/Q123/Q127): landValueBonus becomes a rule and the last two dead catalogue fields are deleted. The field has been on the park since the catalogue was written and landValuePass never read it, so a park reached the ground beside it only through its negative pollution and (since era 10) the leisure coverage layer. It is now deposited over def.radius with coverage's own falloff - 100 per cent at the building, nothing at the radius - by amenityValue() in civic.js, and a RUINED building deposits nothing, because a fire must not improve the neighbourhood. The city hall gains landValueBonus 16 over radius 8 (A91), so six thousand and two hundred a month buys something besides a quest. storage (a water tower that stores nothing: supplyPass allocates per month with no carry-over) and capacity (what a civic building's lit-window fraction would be a share of, which client/world/ may not read - ruling 032) are deleted from the data and the mirror, which leaves UNREAD_FIELDS EMPTY for the first time in the project. The sweep can barely see this rule and that is the honest reading: the deputy builds exactly three bonus carriers a city (one railStation, one marina, one ferryTerminal) and never a park, which is Q133. The MECHANISM is measured beside it, in the same scripted town over 40 seeds with and without parks: before, a park moved land value 63.8 to 97.1 and crime not at all; after, 63.8 to 118.5 with crime 13.3 to 6.7 and population 74 to 86. Crime falls because crimePass reads land value, which is A93's ratified consequence arriving on schedule. Measured with tools/sim_sweep.mjs over 200 games per configuration; see reports/balance-era16.md. ERA 15. G1 (A85, Q116): a network refuses a building, and a grown lot refuses a street. placeNetwork has refused a building on the rail layer alone since A66 (clearOfBuildings on one spec line); road, wire and pipe have been laid straight across one since slice 1.3, which let a player bury their own park under a road and let the deputy's wire cross a coal plant. The rule is now in placeNetwork for every kind, checked before ownership so the answer is needsBulldoze - what to do about it - rather than a permission code. The refusal alone broke the deputy: 169.9 refusals a city on an eight-seed mean and not one avenue, because the avenue is an UPGRADE of the busiest street and that street had houses standing on it. lotFree - placeBuilding's counterpart for a lot nobody placed - never read the road layer, so a block of zoning painted across a street grew lots on the carriageway: 90.9 of 295 buildings a city, for the life of the project. Both halves are one act, measured in three arms: base 90.9 lots on a street and 8.0 avenue tiles; the refusal alone 74.3 and 7.3 with 170 refusals; both 0.0 and 10.0 with none. The price is the third of every city that was illegal - 295 buildings to 238 and population 2,269 to 1,758 on the eight-seed mean. Measured with tools/sim_sweep.mjs over 200 games per configuration; see reports/balance-era15.md. ERA 14. G2 (A86, Q117): the deputy's carriers reach a LIVE grid, for every building it builds rather than for the rail station alone, and it will not put a building where no carrier can arrive. Three defects, each found by the seed the others hid: connectToNetwork joined the NEAREST carrier tile, which is usually a dead stub the deputy laid earlier (seed 404 ended with 228 of 439 buildings holding a pipe and no water while the city held 2,240 capacity against 997 demand); the search started at a lot's top-left tile, which for a 2x2 has two of its own tiles as neighbours, so seed 1003's fire station was sealed in by its own footprint and the run issued nothing and said nothing; and findSpotFor would put a clinic inside a solid block of buildings, which no run can ever reach (seed 404, twice). A spot now needs a side a carrier could ARRIVE at - reachable from the grid, not merely empty, which is the weaker version of the same mistake that seed 1111 showed - and a run that reaches nothing counts itself in deputy.unconnected, because a silent failure is how this lived for the project's life. Over twelve seeds the power grid went from eight components to one and the dark buildings from 60 a city to 0. More carrier is laid for it (1,476 wire tiles to 1,739 on an eight-seed mean), which the city pays for. Measured with tools/sim_sweep.mjs over 200 games per configuration; see reports/balance-era14.md. ERA 13. Q128 (A94): decayOneIn is 3, symmetric with growthOneIn. Era 12 implemented the roll with the 6 that was sitting in the file and nobody had ever chosen either number - decline had been three times faster than growth, and era 12 made it 2.7 times SLOWER (a cut-off lot took eight years to die, against three years to grow through all four levels). At 3 a lot dies in four years and the two forces mirror each other. The lever was measured first: an eight-seed ladder over decayOneIn 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 gave a clean monotone churn column (1,949 / 798 / 492 / 362 / 173 abandonments in 25 years) and a population column that was pure noise at that sample size, which is the project rule about five seeds arriving on schedule. Measured with tools/sim_sweep.mjs over 200 games per configuration; see reports/balance-era13.md. ERA 12. G4 (A92, Q124): decay ROLLS like growth. development.decayOneIn has been in this file since the development pass was written and was read by nothing, so a lot above the growth threshold grew one month in growthOneIn while a lot below the decay threshold lost condition every time it was scored - decline three times as fast as growth, which nobody chose. development.roadWeight and development.crowdingWeight are deleted in the same breath: scoreLot has no such terms and a number nothing reads is a promise rather than a rule. Measured with tools/sim_sweep.mjs over 200 games per configuration; see reports/balance-era12.md. ERA 11. T7 (A70): five cheap rows - clinic, policeHQ, fireHQ, reservoir, wasteFacility - and five deputy considerations, which is why this is an era rather than a catalogue edit. The clinic is the only health a young town can afford and the deputy builds one per deputy.buildingsPerClinic; the headquarters are one-offs past headquartersAtPopulation; the reservoir replaces the pump past reservoirAtPopulation; the tip is built once the city is tipAtPopulation big AND its pollution over developed land passes tipAtPollution (5, which is what the sweep actually reports - the first cut guessed 24 and only ever fired in a village, where two power stations and nine houses is a filthy city by that measure, and it bankrupted every town it fired in: seed 1003 peaked at SIXTY people against 1,260 without it). Measured with tools/sim_sweep.mjs over 200 games per configuration; see reports/balance-era11.md. ERA 10. T6 (A67, A70): leisure and education are coverage layers of their own - tiles.leisure and tiles.education, hashed and saved - fed by five new definitions (plaza, library, stadium, school, university) plus the park and the marina, with a funding row each. They reach the city twice: civic.amenityValueDivisor adds them to land value beside the three departments, and civic.amenityDemand puts the average over DEVELOPED land into the residential pool. The deputy builds a school every deputy.buildingsPerSchool buildings and a plaza every buildingsPerPlaza, so a headless city has both - without that every sweep in the project would have measured a town that reads zero on two of the five layers. Re-measured with tools/sim_sweep.mjs over 200 games per configuration; see reports/balance-era10.md. ERA 9. P87 re-mixed the deputy's OWN stream - Math.imul(seat, 0x9e3779b1) ^ index where era 8 had (seat << 20) + index - inside a review round that changed no rule, and nobody re-ran the sweep. Every deputy decision in every city moved with it, so era 8's report describes a set of worlds that no longer exists: measured at 60 games a side, relaxed's median population went 2275 to 2477, steady's 2415 to 2318, and one steady city died. Re-measured with tools/sim_sweep.mjs over 200 games per configuration; see reports/balance-era9.md. No rule changed; every number moved because the worlds did, which is exactly what era 8 said about itself. T5a arrived in the same commit and is not in it: gate.air and airport.maxDrop are ERA 0, UNTUNED and reach nothing a deputy builds - proved by 60 games a side with and without T5a coming back byte-identical. Numbers from era 8 are void, not roughly comparable. ERA 8. Q113: the deputy draws from its OWN stream, a pure function of the seed, the tick, the seat and the draw's index within the turn, instead of from state.rng - which development, fire and disasters also draw from. One extra deputy action used to shift when every later fire started and every later building grew, so a sweep comparing two eras compared two worlds rather than two rules. No rule changed; every number below moved because the worlds did. ERA 7. T4 (A67, A68): water bodies are derived - a flood over the water layer giving each body a size and whether it reaches a map edge - and three buildings hang off them. A marina needs harbour.marinaMinBody tiles of one body beside it. A ferryTerminal and a freightPort are SEA gates: buildable anywhere a marina is, and LIVE only where the body reaches an edge, which is what gate.sea's terms, its fare and its commuter sink follow. The deputy builds a marina and a terminal past deputy.harbourAtPopulation. ERA 6. T2 (A65, A66, A79): rail is a network of its own, a railStation is a GATE, and worldgen places rock and marsh. A live gate - a station whose line reaches a map edge, powered and with road access - adds gate.rail's integer terms to the regional demand pool, seeds the commuter field as a sink and takes gate.rail.farePerResident from every resident within gate.rail.range. build.rail and upkeep.rail are the line's. ERA 5. T1a (A60): a second road kind. An avenue carries traffic.avenueCapacity times a road before it reads as full, and the commuter field crosses it at traffic.avenueStep against a road traffic.roadStep - so a grid with one avenue routes onto it. build.avenue is its price. ERA 4. B1a (A62): a fire nobody fights spreads and burns slowly rather than dying with the house it started in (fire.unfoughtPercent, unfoughtSpread, unfoughtDamage), and the deputy builds a fire station per deputy.buildingsPerStation buildings - until now it built none, and no gate city in the project has ever had a fire service. Era 3: B9 (A81): the deputy lays a road only within deputy.roadReach tiles of a lot that is built, or zoned and supplied, so a played town grows outward and has an edge; see reports/balance-era3.md. Era 2 is left to T1/T2's re-pin (A79). Otherwise unchanged from era 1 — ERA 1. Tuned 2026-08-29 against tools/sim_sweep.mjs over 200 games per configuration; see reports/balance-era1.md. Changed from era 0: civic.pollutionAverage now averages over developed land instead of the whole region, so it reads 9 instead of 0 and can drive something. RE-TESTED AND REJECTED, for the second time: per-tile wire and pipe upkeep. At 1 each it put p25 treasury on 0 and cut p25 population from 647 to 187 — it bankrupts weak cities without touching the rich ones, which is what the era-0 note already said. ACCEPTED, not fixed: runaway treasuries, median 1.9M and p95 3.8M after 25 years. Numbers from era 0 are void, not roughly comparable.

build._bridge: S13 (A84, A111): how many tiles of water one crossing may span. The engine has always allowed a road over water and charged roadOverWater for it - A84 believed otherwise because no 64x64 deputy city had ever paved one, and H7's played 96 has ten such tiles - so the rule S13 adds is a SPAN and an end on dry land, not permission. Six tiles is 120 m, which is a river rather than a lake: the renderer gives the run a deck at a fixed height with a ramp either end inside road.maxGrade, and a ramp that long at 15% is already 18 m of climb.

difficulty._demanding: J4 (A106, Q141): demanding's squeeze, re-cut against a real expense. taxYieldPercent 80 and upkeepPercent 120 were set in era 1, when a developed lot cost nothing to serve - so demanding had nothing to absorb H8's service cost with, and the lever shipped at a third of what it was worth (3/6/11/18 instead of 6/12/22/35, because the 200-game sweep lost nine demanding cities of two hundred at the higher rung). Measured over FORTY demanding cities a rung: at 80/120 with the service cost doubled the population is 1,207 and four cities die; at 90/110 it is 1,516 with none, which is the population demanding has today (1,547) and a p25 treasury of 1,676k against 1,616k. So the squeeze comes in by a third and the service cost doubles, and demanding ends where it started with a real expense inside it. 95/105 was measured too and is too kind (2,457k p25); 12/25/45/70 still kills cities at every squeeze tried, which is where this lever stops.

gate._comment: T2 (A65): the Outside is gate buildings, not a second simulation. A LIVE gate adds these integer terms to the regional demand pool, seeds the commuter field as a sink, and takes a fare from every resident within range. ERA 0, UNTUNED against the bases in `demand` below (400/150/150).

air._comment: T5 (A69): the largest terms there are, plus a LANDING FEE - a flat monthly sum a live airport earns from the aircraft rather than from the residents near it, which is why an airport in an empty region is still worth something. ERA 0, UNTUNED.

airport._comment: T5 (A69). maxDrop is the largest difference in `tiles.elevation` the airport's footprint may contain - a runway is flat, and the engine has no metres. Six units is three metres at the renderer's half-metre relief step, a tenth of the grade a road is allowed over the same 120 m, because a road climbs and a runway does not. On a rolling map about one 6x4 site in ten qualifies; on a hilly one almost none, which is the intent.

harbour._comment: T4 (A67, A68). marinaMinBody is how many tiles of one body a marina needs beside it - a pond is not a harbour. `water` next to this is the UTILITY's, and a second block of that name silently replaced it. ERA 0, UNTUNED.

development._slope: H6 (A100): the steepest step in elevation units between a tile and a four-neighbour that may still be zoned. Six, because that is the grade a STREET may climb: road.maxGrade is 15%, a tile is 20 m and an elevation step is 0.5 m, so 15% of 20 m is 3 m is six steps. You may not zone ground a street could not be built on. Measured over three 128 maps a style: it leaves rolling at 100% of its buildable tiles (93% are at 4 or less) and flat at 100%, and takes hilly from 100% to 41% - which is the point, and is still 17,000 tiles of city.
development._plinth: A120 (Q144): the elevation SPREAD a building's footprint may stand on, in steps. A building is seated on the lowest corner of its lot and a plinth makes up the difference (ruling 038) - so on a hillside the ground at the lot's middle climbs to the roof and what is drawn is a building in the hill with a wall of base below it. S12 cut the natural shore and left exactly this: the hard edges at a waterline are lots on their plinths. Eight steps is four metres, a storey and a half - a basement level on a slope reads, and past it the building is buried: walkthrough's four 'walked into' lots on hilly 128 are each 16 steps, with the walker's feet within 15 cm of a roof. Measured over three played cities: flat 64 has a maximum spread of 1 step and loses nothing; rolling 96 has 11 of 284 buildings over 4 steps and NONE over 8, so it loses nothing either; hilly 128 has 31 of 185 over 4, 19 over 8 and 7 over 16, and the worst are the big civic footprints - a 3x3 coal plant at 28 steps is fourteen metres. So the rule bites hilly ground and only hilly ground, which is where the picture is wrong.
development._roadSlope: J3 (A112): the steepest step ALONG a run that may still be paved, in elevation units. A lot refuses ground too rough to stand on - maxZoneSlope, the max step to any neighbour - and a road refuses a CLIMB too steep to drive, which is the step between consecutive tiles of the run; a street along a contour across a hillside has a gentle grade and a steep neighbour, and the first cut used the lot's test and took a played hilly city from 1,872 residents to 217. Twelve steps is six metres over a twenty-metre tile, about 30%: steeper than a street may be GRADED (road.maxGrade 15%), because this is the land a street may be laid ACROSS and S11's grading then flattens the street within its corridor. Measured as a ladder over four 64 maps a style, 25 years, with walkthrough 128 hilly beside it: rolling is unmoved from 10 upward; hilly reads 6 -> 147 residents, 10 -> 697, 11 -> 1,094, 12 -> 1,066, 13 -> 964, 14 -> 1,711, 20 and no limit -> 1,342. Fourteen beats NO LIMIT by a quarter - a deputy that stops at the foot of a hill builds where the city can be served - and fails the gate on one marginal cliff (1.03 m against a 1.00 m threshold). Twelve is the rung where walkthrough 128 hilly goes GREEN for the first time in the project: 0 cliffs, 0 refusals, 20 of 177 corridors ungradeable against 218 of 612, steepest street 500% -> 33.3%. The gate is what A112 named as the measurement, so the gate chose the number.

economy._service: H8 (A101, Q118): what a developed lot costs the city to SERVE, per level. Until era 21 a lot was pure income - it paid tax and cost nothing - while the only expenses were the civic buildings and a penny a road tile, so a steady 25-year city took 20,268 a month and spent 5,048, banked the rest for twenty-five years and ended on 4.7 million. Per-TILE upkeep was tried twice and rejected twice because it bankrupts a young town without touching a rich one; this scales with what the city HAS GROWN rather than with what it has paved, so a village of nine level-1 cottages pays 225 a month and a city of 160 lots pays seven thousand. The ladder is steep on purpose - a level-4 tower is four cottages' worth of water, refuse and road - and it is calibrated from the lot census of a 25-year steady city (45/29/13/8 residential by level, 17/7/1 commercial, 29/9/2 industrial) and it is chosen from a four-rung ladder measured over eight cities a difficulty: at 0 the treasuries are 6,466k relaxed / 5,021k steady / 2,534k demanding; at 6/12/22/35 they are 5,837k / 4,264k / 1,258k with nobody dead; at 12/25/45/70 DEMANDING COLLAPSES, from 1,644 residents to 163 with a city dead of eight. The useful range of this lever is bounded by demanding's margin, not by the mechanism - it pays 120% of every expense and keeps 80% of every tax, so it has nothing to absorb a new one with. The eight-seed ladder said 6/12/22/35 killed nobody and the 200-game SWEEP said nine demanding cities of two hundred reached a hundred residents and ended empty - never tune on five seeds, from the other direction - so the rung came down again: at 3/6/11/18, measured over FORTY demanding cities, the dead count is 0, the population is 1,618 against 1,632 and the treasury 1,955k against 2,374k. A first step, deliberately small, and the reason it is small is demanding's own margin - J4 (A106) re-cuts it and raises this.

fire._unfought: B1a (A62): a fire is unaddressed when at least unfoughtPercent of the building's own fire risk is left after coverage - no station in range - and it then spreads unfoughtSpread times as readily while consuming its house more slowly, so it outlives what it is standing on and reaches the next one.

disasters._comment: era 0, untuned. Frequency is difficulty.disasterOneIn, which already existed; this is only the shape of one.

traffic._comment: era 0, untuned. roadCapacity is load units per tile before a street reads as full.

deputy._comment: A81 (B9): the deputy lays a road only within roadReach tiles of a lot that is built, or zoned and supplied; expand reaches a little further than the doctrines that hold back. Era 3. T2: railAtPopulation is the size at which it lays a line to the edge and puts a station on it - just above avenueAtPopulation, so the order is the main road first and the railway after it.
deputy._blockTiles: B14 (era 29): a street is refused where most of its run already has a parallel street within this many tiles. The deputy laid a run wherever its cursor stood, and the cursor hops -2..2 tiles across, so two streets could be laid side by side: 31-40% of a played 64 was road against the references' 4-13% of a frame. Refused rather than moved - a deputy that shuffles until it finds a gap paves the same amount more slowly - and 'most', not 'any', because a new street legitimately starts beside an old one and leaves it.
deputy._bridge: A121 (Q143): the deputy goes looking for a crossing. S13 taught buildBlockAlong to span a river its block happens to meet and measured what that is worth - in a twenty-year played 96 the deputy meets water fifteen times and a building on the far bank refused all five attempts, so it built none. Everything else structural it owns is sought on purpose: a line past railAtPopulation, a harbour past harbourAtPopulation. bridgeAtPopulation is the same shape, bridgeCap is how many it may seek in one game, and bridgeNeedsRoom is what makes it worth doing - free unzoned tiles within bridgeRoomReach of where the bridge LANDS, because a crossing onto a rock is a crossing to nowhere and this rule exists to open land.

loan._note: L1 (A130): the ceiling is a ladder by RANK, so a town that has earned nothing can still borrow a little and a city that has earned its rank can borrow enough to matter. Interest is per thousand per MONTH, integer: 6 per 1000 is 7.2% a year, which is dear enough that a loan is a decision and cheap enough that it is a way out. The deputy never borrows (it is the measurement instrument), so these numbers do not move the sweep - which is the claim era 28 is for.
